title: Why Are There So Many Denominations?
excerpt: Jesus prayed that his followers would be one so that the world would believe, and the history of why they are not includes pride, slavery, honest conviction and a prayer that is still unanswered.
body:
A woman new to town drives down one road and passes six churches, each with a different name on the sign, and can't tell from the signs whether they are rivals, cousins or strangers. A man raised in one of them marries a woman raised in another, and the two families discover at the wedding that they are not sure whether they can take communion together. A boy asks his grandfather why the family doesn't go to the big church on the corner, and the grandfather finds that the true answer is a quarrel older than he is, which he has never looked into.

The skeptic has a simpler way of putting it. Jesus said his followers would be known by their love for one another. The church says the Holy Spirit leads it into truth. Christians can't agree on baptism, on bread and wine, on who is in charge, or on which building to stand in while they disagree, and in the centuries when they had armies they settled such questions with armies. If this is what the Spirit's guidance produces, the skeptic says, the claim of guidance isn't worth much.

That charge can't be waved away. Jesus himself gave the world the right to make it. On the night before he died he prayed for everyone who would ever believe in him, "that they may all be one," and he gave the reason: "so that the world may believe that you have sent me" (John 17:21). He made the unity of his people a piece of evidence, so their division counts as evidence against them.

## Older Than the Signs

The trouble did not start with Protestants. It is in the New Testament. Within about twenty-five years of the resurrection Paul was writing to a single congregation that had already sorted itself into parties. "Each one of you says, 'I follow Paul,' or 'I follow Apollos,' or 'I follow Cephas,' or 'I follow Christ.' Is Christ divided?" (1 Corinthians 1:12–13). Paul and Barnabas, who had planted churches together, had "a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other" (Acts 15:39). Paul once opposed Peter to his face in front of a whole church (Galatians 2:11).

The New Testament also shows what the apostles thought unity was. It was a fact before it was a task: "one body and one Spirit," "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all" (Ephesians 4:4–6). And it was to be kept by effort, because it could be damaged: Paul asks his readers to be "eager to maintain the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace" (Ephesians 4:3). The creed the churches still share says the same in four words when it confesses "one holy catholic and apostolic Church." Every Christian who recites that line on Sunday is confessing a church that he cannot see from the parking lot.

For centuries the church treated breaking away as among the worst of sins. Cyprian, bishop of Carthage in the middle of the third century, wrote the sentence that summed it up: "He can no longer have God for his Father, who has not the Church for his mother." His question has stayed with the church ever since, because it assumes that everyone knows where the church is.

## The Three Great Breaks

The first lasting division came in the fifth century and is the one Western Christians know least. In 451 the Council of Chalcedon confessed Christ as one person in two natures, divine and human. Most of the church received it. Ancient churches in Egypt, Syria and farther east did not, and the site's history course says plainly that the council "split off ancient communions in Egypt and Syria and the East that have never returned." Those churches are still there. They confess that Christ is fully God and fully man, and they have worshiped apart from the rest for fifteen hundred years over how to say it.

The second break is dated 1054 and was centuries in coming. The Greek-speaking East and the Latin-speaking West had drifted apart in language, in politics and in their view of the bishop of Rome's authority. The sharpest issue was one word. The creed agreed by the councils said the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. Churches in the West added "and the Son." The West meant to guard the full deity of the Son. The East objected to the teaching and objected as much to the manner, since no one region had the right to alter the common confession of all. In 1054 a papal delegate laid a document of excommunication on the altar of the great church in Constantinople, and the patriarch answered in kind. At the time many Christians barely noticed. What made the break permanent came a hundred and fifty years later, when a Western crusading army sacked Constantinople itself in 1204, looting its churches and killing fellow Christians. The East had seen what the West would do, and it did not forget.

The West then divided against itself before any Protestant existed. In the fourteenth century the papacy sat for most of a hundred years at Avignon under the French crown, and after that came rival popes, first two and then three, "each excommunicating the others' obediences, while ordinary believers were left to guess where the church even was." That was a century before Luther.

The third break began on October 31, 1517, when a German monk named Martin Luther posted ninety-five theses for debate on the sale of indulgences. He did not set out to found a church. He believed the gospel of grace had been buried under a system of payments and penalties, and he called the church he loved to reform. In 1521, before the emperor, he was told to take it back, and he answered that his conscience was captive to the Word of God. He was excommunicated. Those who agreed with him did not think they had left the church. They thought they were the church, put out of doors for saying what Paul said.

Rome saw it another way, and that view should be given in its own terms too. A single monk had set his private reading of Scripture above the judgment of the whole church across fifteen centuries, and if he might do it, so might anyone. Rome reformed a good deal in the decades that followed. The sellers of pardons whose trade had lit the fuse were abolished. But it held that the remedy for a sick church could never be a second church.

Under the quarrel about indulgences lay a disagreement about what the unity of the church is, and it has never been settled. For Rome, the one church is a visible body in communion with the bishop of Rome. For the Orthodox, it is the churches that hold the faith of the ancient councils in communion with one another. The Protestant confessions located it in the gospel itself, and spoke of a church that only God can count: "The catholic or universal Church, which is invisible, consists of the whole number of the elect." Each of the three can explain the other two as the ones who left. That is part of why goodwill alone has not ended the division.

## Why Protestants Kept Dividing

Rome's warning proved accurate in one respect. Twelve years after the theses, the two leading reformers met at Marburg to unite their movements, agreed on fourteen articles of fifteen, and parted over the Lord's Supper. In Zurich, students of the Reformation concluded that baptism belongs to believers only, and were drowned for it by other Protestants. In England the break with Rome began with a king's marriage and became a long struggle over how far reform should go, which in time produced Puritans, separatists and dissenters of several kinds. The site's history course says that Protestantism learned at Marburg "the skill it has practiced ever since: dividing over real differences among those who agree on almost everything, and calling the division faithfulness."

For a century and more the divisions were settled by force. The peace made in 1555 let each ruler choose the religion of his territory, so that a person's faith was assigned by his government and a troubled conscience could only move away. From 1618 to 1648 central Europe fought a war that began over that settlement and ended, in the course's words, with the argument "buried under a generation of the baptized dead."

That history explains the word on the signs. A denomination is a named part of the church that does not claim to be the whole of it. The idea took hold where governments stopped enforcing one church, and most of all in America, where no church was established by the nation and every church had to persuade. The course calls the result "a religious free market." Its gains were real. Nobody was drowned for his baptism, and the gospel reached people the established churches had ignored. Its costs were real too. A church that must win a crowd is tempted to give the crowd what it wants, and where every reader is his own final court, a disagreement is easily turned into a new congregation. More than one American movement set out to end the divisions by going back to the Bible alone, and found, as the course puts it, that "the Bible alone, read alone, yields as many Christianities as there are readers." Many churches side by side are, in part, what Christians learned to do when they stopped killing one another. Nobody should take that for the unity Jesus prayed for, but it was better than what came before it.

## Which Divisions Were Sin

It would be easy to say that all division is sin and stop there. The history doesn't allow it, because the divisions were not all of one kind.

Some came from pride. The course's judgment on 1054 is that "two proud men lost their tempers in a single building." The sack of 1204 was a crime by any measure.

Some came from sin that had nothing to do with doctrine. In 1844 and 1845 the two largest evangelical bodies in America, the Methodists and the Baptists, each tore in half, and the occasion in both cases was whether a man could hold slaves and serve the church as a bishop or a missionary. The southern bodies were organized so that he could. Around 1787, in Philadelphia, as Richard Allen later told it, Black members of a Methodist church were pulled up from their knees during prayer by white trustees who told them they were in the wrong seats. They walked out together, and in 1816 the first fully independent Black denomination in the United States was organized. That division was caused by sin, and the people who left did not commit it. They are the reason "division" and "sin" can't be treated as the same word. More than one American denomination exists because one set of Christians would not sit beside another.

Some came from conviction held in good conscience on both sides. Christians who baptize infants and Christians who baptize only believers can't do both in one congregation. Neither can a church be governed by bishops and by its own members at once. These are second-order questions. They don't divide the faith, and yet a congregation has to settle them one way to function at all. Two essays on this site take up [baptism](/writing/babies-or-believers-why-christians-baptize-differently) and [the Lord's Supper](/writing/what-is-the-lords-supper). Separate churches over such questions may be the least bad arrangement available, provided that each knows the other to be the church.

Paul made room for this kind of difference inside a single congregation. Writing to Christians who disagreed about food and holy days, he did not rule for either side. "Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind," he said, and then, "Why do you pass judgment on your brother?" (Romans 14:5, 10). The churches have found that harder to practice than he made it sound.

And a great many came from nothing so dignified. Paul's word for this was blunt: "while there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not of the flesh and behaving only in a human way?" (1 Corinthians 3:3).

The same four causes can be found in any one church's history, the reader's included, and usually more than one of them at a time. Most of us inherited our sign from a quarrel we have never examined, and we defend it as if we had chosen it.

## What Is Still Held in Common

The skeptic's picture of thousands of competing religions misses how much is shared. The Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, and the ancient churches that parted at Chalcedon, confess one God who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit. They confess Jesus Christ as truly God and truly man, crucified for sinners and raised bodily on the third day. They read the same Gospels and the same letters of Paul. They baptize in the same threefold name, pray the same prayer Jesus taught, and keep the same meal, however differently they explain it. Nearly all of them can say the creed of the fourth-century councils, one disputed clause aside, without crossing their fingers.

The Protestant confessions, written in the heat of the divisions, were more modest than their heirs have often been. The Lutheran confession of 1530 says that "to the true unity of the Church it is enough to agree concerning the doctrine of the Gospel and the administration of the Sacraments," and that ceremonies need not "be everywhere alike." The Westminster Confession says of every church on earth, its own included, "The purest churches under heaven are subject both to mixture and error." No church that signed that sentence may behave as if it were the exception.

In 1965 the pope and the patriarch of Constantinople lifted the excommunications of 1054. It did not end the division. It was done as a gesture of repentance, nine hundred years late, and it showed that the anathemas of one century need not bind the next.

## Living on a Road With Six Churches

None of this tells the woman new to town which door to walk through, and this essay will not tell her. It can tell her what to look for behind any of them: the creed confessed, the Scriptures read and obeyed, the gospel of grace preached, baptism and the Supper kept, and people who love one another and the stranger. Where those are, the church is, whatever the sign says.

It can also say what belonging to one of them does not license. It does not license contempt for the others. The disciples once tried to stop a man who was doing good in Jesus' name "because he was not following us," and Jesus told them, "the one who is not against us is for us" (Mark 9:38, 40). A Christian can hold his own church's convictions with a whole heart and still know that the church down the road was baptized into the same Lord. He can grieve the wall and keep his convictions too.

On the night he prayed that they would be one, Jesus knew what kind of men he was praying for. Earlier that evening they had been arguing about which of them was the greatest. He prayed it anyway, and then he went out to die for all of them at once.

That prayer has not yet been answered in any way the world can see. It is among the oldest unanswered prayers the church knows, and it was prayed by Christ himself. Every sign on that road is a record of why. The woman driving past is still waiting to see what he said she would see.

*"I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word, that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me."* (John 17:20–21)

*"Is Christ divided?"* (1 Corinthians 1:13)
